papers.title: Polyvinylpyrrolidone-Based Bio-Ink Improves Cell Viability and Homogeneity during Drop-On-Demand Printing.
papers.abstract: Drop-on-demand (DOD) bioprinting has attracted huge attention for numerous biological applications due to its precise control over material volume and deposition pattern in a contactless printing approach. 3D bioprinting is still an emerging field and more work is required to improve the viability and homogeneity of printed cells during the printing process. Here, a general purpose bio-ink was developed using polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) macromolecules. Different PVP-based bio-inks (0%-3% w/v) were prepared and evaluated for their printability; the short-term and long-term viability of the printed cells were first investigated. The Z value of a bio-ink determines its printability; it is the inverse of the Ohnesorge number (Oh), which is the ratio between the Reynolds number and a square root of the Weber number, and is independent of the bio-ink velocity. The viability of printed cells is dependent on the Z values of the bio-inks; the results indicated that the cells can be printed without any significant impairment using a bio-ink with a threshold Z value of ≤9.30 (2% and 2.5% w/v). Next, the cell output was evaluated over a period of 30 min. The results indicated that PVP molecules mitigate the cell adhesion and sedimentation during the printing process; the 2.5% w/v PVP bio-ink demonstrated the most consistent cell output over a period of 30 min. Hence, PVP macromolecules can play a critical role in improving the cell viability and homogeneity during the bioprinting process.

papers.title: Low dose effect of bisphosphonates on hMSCs osteogenic response to titanium surface in vitro
papers.abstract: Since the 1980s, titanium (Ti) implants have been routinely used to replace missing teeth. This success is mainly due to the good biocompatibility of Ti and the phenomenon of osseointegration, with very early events at implant placement being important in determining good osseointegration. However, enhancing implant performance with coatings such as hydroxyapatite (HA) and calcium phosphate has proved largely unsuccessful. Human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) are the first osteogenic cells to colonise implant surfaces and offer a target for enhancing osseointegration. We previously reported that small doses of bisphosphonate (BP) may play an integral role in enhancing hMSC proliferation and osteogenic differentiation. The aim of this study is to investigate whether small doses of bisphosphonates enhance proliferation and osteogenic differentiation of hMSCs on Ti surfaces, to enhance bone osseointegration and to accelerate wound healing around the implant surface. Our data suggests that treating cells with small doses of BP (100 nM & 10 nM) induces significant hMSC stimulation of osteogenic markers including calcium, collagen type I and ALP compared to control group on titanium surfaces (P < 0.05). In addition, cell proliferation and migration were significantly enhanced on titanium surfaces (P < 0.05).

papers.title: Effect of ridge preservation for early implant placement – is there a need to remove the biomaterial?
papers.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess (i) bone regeneration around implants placed early in sites with or without ridge preservation and (ii) if the bone substitute material ( DBBM ‐C) has to be removed at implant placement. Materials and methods In eight beagle dogs, three sites were randomly assigned to ridge preservation ( DBBM ‐C plus collagen matrix ( CMX )) (two sites; RP ) or spontaneous healing (1 site; SH ). Four weeks later, in one of the RP sites, dental implants were placed without removing the DBBM ‐C ( RP 1), whereas in RP 2 and SH sites all non‐integrated DBBM ‐C and/or granulation tissue were removed before implant placement and concomitant GBR . Histomorphometric outcomes were assessed at 4 and 12 weeks. Results The median buccal fBIC (first bone‐to‐implant contact) was located more apical in groups RP 1: 1.34 mm (0.09; 2.96) and RP 2: 1.41 mm (0.54; 2.72) than in group SH : 0.79 mm (0.26; 1.50) ( p = 0.452) at 4 weeks. At 12 weeks, median buccal fBIC values were for RP 1: 0.88 mm (0.00; 2.33), for RP 2: 0.16 mm (0.00; 1.33) and for SH : 0.00 mm (0.00; 0.98) ( p = 0.362). BIC values increased over 12 weeks in all groups. Conclusions Ridge preservation followed by early implant placement led to higher BIC values at 12 than at 4 weeks. There is no need to remove the biomaterial at implant placement to ensure osseointegration. No relevant differences were observed between the three groups for any outcome measure.

papers.title: Hybrid Implants in Healthy and Periodontally Compromised Patients: A Preliminary Clinical and Radiographic Study
papers.abstract: This preliminary clinical and radiographic study examined the survival of, the marginal bone loss (MBL) around, and the influence of prosthetic abutment height (AH) on MBL around hybrid implants placed in two groups of partially edentulous patients: healthy (HPs) and periodontally compromised (PCPs) patients. A total of 93 patients requiring single or multiunit implant restoration, in the mandible or maxilla, were treated while undergoing cement-retained prosthetic restoration. A total of 54 implants (35 in the maxilla and 19 in the mandible) were placed in 45 HPs, and 56 implants (31 in the maxilla and 25 in the mandible) in 48 PCPs. All 110 hybrid implants positioned in pristine bone provided a 100% survival rate in both HPs and PCPs. No statistical differences were recorded comparing the MBL values of maxillae with those of mandibles. In HPs and PCPs, a similar and limited amount of MBL was recorded, and it was found that the higher the AH, the less MBL. In conclusion, results indicate that the hybrid implants examined could reduce the risk of peri-implantitis due to their coronal machined surfaces and improve osseointegration due to their apical rough surfaces.

papers.title: Three-Dimensional Microstructured Lattices for Oil Sensing
papers.abstract: Monitoring of environmental contamination, including oil pollution, is important to protect marine ecosystems. A wide range of sensors are used in the petroleum industry to measure various parameters, such as viscosity, pressure, and flow. Here, we create an optical lattice mesh structure that can be used as an oil sensor integrated with optical fiber probing. The principle of operation of the sensor was based on light scattering, where the tested medium acted as a diffuser. Three different mesh-patterned structures were analyzed by optical imaging, light transmission, and scattering in the presence of supercut, diesel, and stroke oil types. The meshes were used as a medium for different types of oils, and the optical diffusion and transmission were studied in the visible spectrum. Angle-resolved measurements were carried out to characterize the light scattering behavior from the mesh structures. Different types of oils were identified on the basis of the optical behavior of the lattice structure. The fabricated mesh structures can be used as a low-cost measurement device in oil sensing.

Originally published17 Feb 2017https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCRESAHA.116.310051Circulation Research. 2017;120:630–632A long-standing goal of cardiovascular scientists is to repair damaged hearts after myocardial infarction by overcoming the limited regenerative capacity of the adult mammalian heart. Many new strategies are being actively investigated for generating functional cardiomyocytes or progenitor cells. The race is on for the first demonstration of durable therapeutic heart repair in human.The classical paradigm that the adult mammalian heart is a postmitotic, terminally differentiated organ has been actively debated. Data from 14C dating studies have demonstrated a limited self-renewal capacity of the adult mammalian heart that declines with age.1 These repair processes are, however, insufficient to compensate for extensive cell loss occurring after acute or chronic cardiac injury. Therefore, investigators in cardiovascular regenerative medicine have actively explored different approaches to replace the postinfarct scar tissue with contractile muscle cells. Despite these efforts, a central question for the field of cardiac regenerative medicine remains: what strategy will take us to the finish line in this race to achieve complete heart regeneration? In this Viewpoint article, we comment on recent experimental and clinical approaches to regenerate the failing heart and highlight the urgent need to clarify the biology of cardiomyocyte (CM) development, growth, and maturation.Mechanisms of Endogenous RegenerationThe mammalian heart harbors multiple cell types that may be targeted in regenerative strategies. Conceptually, the most direct approach is to stimulate pre-existing CMs to re-enter the cell cycle. Alternatively, resident cardiomyogenic stem/progenitor cell populations have been described to differentiate directly into CMs. Although there are advantages and disadvantages to each approach, it is clear that both strategies have demonstrated early promises that require further improvement and independent validation in nonrodent models.Induction of Cardiomyocyte DivisionNeonatal HeartThe regenerative capacity of the neonatal mammalian heart seems to be greater than that of adult heart because of the presence of a short window of CM proliferative competence.2 Immediately after birth, the neonatal mouse heart harbors some regenerative potential, although ongoing debate remains about the exact degree of regeneration. Neonatal regeneration in the human heart has been suggested by newborn children with acute myocardial infarction.3 However, whether this recovery involves CM regeneration versus ventricular unloading and early revascularization requires further validation. With regard to the signaling pathways that might activate neonatal CM division, it has been reported that Meis1 and neuregulin-1 play important roles.2,4 The finding of extensive CM proliferation seen in Hippo pathway knockout animals raises exciting prospect for future therapies.5Adult HeartDuring physiological homeostasis in human, the number of new adult CMs generated is estimated to be ≈1% per year.1 This rate declines with age but likely increases after injury. D'Uva et al6 recently reported the induction of binucleated CM proliferation by constitutive activation of the ERBB2 receptor. Interestingly, this approach results in cardiac hypertrophy and CM proliferation in the neonatal heart and CM dedifferentiation, proliferation, and redifferentiation in the adult heart.Recruitment of Endogenous Stem/Progenitor CellsThe role of endogenous stem/progenitor cells to mediate heart repair or regeneration has garnered intense interest among cardiovascular investigators. This coincided with the rising interest in stem cell biology in general in the past 2 decades and the hope that this alternative approach may be more efficient in generating new CMs in the diseased heart than trying to force a mitotically inactive adult CM to re-enter the cell cycle.Resident Cardiac Stem CellMany different cell populations within the adult heart expressing markers such as Sca-1, c-Kit, Hoechst dye exclusion (ie, side population), or PDGFRα have been studied for their cardiomyogenic potential.7 In most cases, these cells were shown to turn on sarcomeric protein genes under in vitro culturing conditions, and their identity as a stem/progenitor cell for CMs has been proposed based on these data. Given the limited cell engraftment/survival after transplantation, it has been challenging to assess the degree of their differentiation into functional CMs in vivo. Recent lineage-tracing data have raised the possibility that few c-Kit–expressing cells give rise to adult CMs in the murine heart.8 Intriguingly, a large number of c-Kit+ cells in the adult heart may represent endothelial cells, and a rare number of these may undergo CM conversion.9Circulating Stem/Progenitor CellThe bone marrow, spleen, and the liver can serve as reservoir for hematopoietic stem or progenitor cells that respond and migrate to the site of myocardial injury via circulation. Although these cells seem to provide important cytokines/growth factors for cardiac repair, they do not become CMs by direct differentiation.10 Recently, Wu et al11 used a murine parabiosis model to show that a small number of circulating cells adopted cardiovascular cell fate via cell fusion, whereas an even smaller (<0.1%) number of cells result from transdifferentiation. It seems that cell fusion as a strategy for generating new proliferative cardiomyocytes would require a significant increase in efficiency to be effective for repairing the ≈1 billion lost cardiomyocytes after a large infarction.Transplantation of Exogenous CellsA wealth of basic and clinical studies in the past 2 decades has examined the consequences of autologous cell transplantation to regenerate the damaged heart. Although many issues have been explored, it remains unclear whether there is an optimal cell type that can regenerate the damaged heart after transplantation. Given the space constraint, we refer the readers to other excellent review article on this topic and instead focus our discussion to studies involving transplantation of pluripotent stem cell–derived CMs as a potential strategy for remuscularizing post-MI hearts.Pluripotent Stem Cell–Derived Cardiac CellsMouse and human embryonic stem cells (ESCs) have demonstrated remarkable capacity to differentiate into multiple key cardiac cell types in the body. However, the use of human ESCs (hESCs) for research or clinical purposes has raised ethical concerns. The establishment of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) by somatic reprogramming circumvented many of these ethical challenges. Although iPSCs have proven to be a robust alternative to ESCs, questions about their risk of teratoma formation remain. Furthermore, hiPSC-derived CMs are fetal-like and immature so may not fully recapitulate the adult mature CM physiology required for proper function. Nevertheless, there has been significant progress in the transplantation of human ESC- or iPSC-derived cardiac cells by either direct injection or a cardiac patch.By Direct InjectionWith regard to transplantation of hESC-derived CMs (hESC-CMs), a series of studies in rodents followed by large animal models have led to the first demonstration of hESC-CMs transplantation into a nonhuman primate model.12 These GCaMP-labeled hESC-CMs (≈109 cells) were intramyocardially injected into infarcted macaque hearts. The investigators showed that a fraction of the injected CMs integrated into the host myocardium by histological assessment and were electrically coupled to the native rhythm. Interestingly, there was an increased incidence of nonfatal ventricular arrhythmias during the first 2 to 4 weeks after transplantation. Further studies will be needed to reduce the frequency of ventricular arrhythmia and assess whether the engrafted cells contribute to cardiac function in the long term.Via Engineered Cardiac PatchTo overcome the challenges associated with cell survival after transplantation, investigators have explored the creation of bioengineered tissues using cells or soluble factors. A recent study demonstrated the delivery of human ESC-derived cardiac cells in cardiac patches into ischemic cardiomyopathy patients.13 Although not designed as an efficacy study, the reported improvement of left ventricular ejection fraction from 26% to 36% by echocardiography is encouraging. Importantly, no arrhythmia, teratoma formation, or immunosuppression-related events were observed. Many issues on the use of bioengineered patches will need to be resolved. These includes the need for a well-developed vascular network for cell survival, electrically synchronizing the transplanted cells with the native myocardium, and, ideally, a less invasive way to introduce these patches so that the number of patients eligible to receive this treatment is not limited to the ones who are undergoing an open-chest surgery. We anticipate that new engineering breakthroughs such as 3-dimensional bioprinting, decellularized cardiac matrix, or novel nanoparticles will help to move the field forward.Direct Reprogramming StrategiesDistinct from the reprogramming of adult somatic cells into iPSCs, the direct reprogramming of one adult cell type into another, without passing through a pluripotent state, has been vigorously pursued in recent years. A theoretical advantage of this approach is the availability of a larger population of fibroblasts in a post-MI heart that can be targeted and the avoidance of teratoma risk.Conversion of Fibroblasts Into CardiomyocytesBy the overexpression of 3 cardiac transcription factors (Gata4, Mef2c, and Tbx5), Ieda et al14 reported the generation of induced CMs in vitro. This study was subsequently followed by studies reporting the conversion of cardiac fibroblasts into CMs in vivo. Additional follow-on studies have identified new transcription factors, microRNAs, and delivery methods to improve the efficiency of fibroblasts conversion to CMs; however, questions remain as to whether this method will be efficient enough to generate the large number of CMs needed for complete regeneration and whether the reprogramming methods in animal models would work as well in humans without using oncogenic viral vectors.Conversion of Fibroblasts Into Cardiac Progenitor CellsGiven the limited proliferation of differentiated CMs, it has become of interest to directly reprogram fibroblasts into cardiac progenitor cells (CPCs) that can proliferate and differentiate into all major cardiac lineages. Recently, Lalit et al15 reported the generation of tripotent CPCs by introducing Gata4, Nkx2.5, Tbx5, Mesp1, and Baf60c into fibroblasts via lentiviruses. The authors reported improvement in cardiac function after transplantation of these induced CPCs into infarcted mouse hearts. It remains to be determined whether the cardiac functional improvement is directly related to the generation of new CMs from induced CPCs or from an injection paracrine effect. Furthermore, it would be of interest to see whether this phenomenon holds true during in vivo induced CPC reprogramming.Summary and Future PerspectiveThe number and variety of promising approaches to address the failing heart via endogenous and exogenous stem cells and direct CM targeting clearly reflects the clinical need (Figure). Although it remains to be seen which treatment approach will result in the best outcome with the least toxicity, each of these strategies has demonstrated advantages and disadvantages in preclinical studies that warrant further investigation. Although currently it is unclear which of the various strategies described in this article will prevail, the cardiac regeneration race seems to be in full swing. We anticipate that a significantly greater understanding of the biology of CM development and differentiation will be necessary to achieve this worthwhile goal.Download figureDownload PowerPointFigure. papers.title: Developing Studio Spaces as Catalysts for Innovative and Collaborative Pedagogy
papers.abstract: As higher education shifts to meet the needs of modern students and employers, libraries have become much more than spaces to hold a collection of books. Both the media and the functions of the spaces have changed, and studio or lab spaces are one way that libraries are better able to support work with digital media from both student (Mandel, 2008) and faculty (Bailey, Blunt, & Magner, 2011) perspectives. In this session, attendees will consider why creating studio or lab spaces to support pedagogically-driven learning is important for all institutions and how one might take steps to begin designing or encouraging the creation of this kind of space. Additionally, attendees will explore strategies for finding and partnering with the labs/studios that may already be available on their campuses. We assert that, through these partnerships, both the studios and faculty can grow and better support engaging, active learning throughout the campus community.
